found-communication-l01.q: You are about to place a blood pressure cuff on a shaking, tearful patient. What should you do in the two seconds before you inflate it?
choices: Inflate quickly so it is over sooner
Tell her the cuff is going to squeeze her arm tightly for a few seconds
Ask her four screening questions while it inflates
Tell her there is nothing to worry about
found-communication-l01.why: Announcing a sensation before it happens is what stops a frightened patient from jerking away. Speed does not reduce surprise, stacked questions overload a narrowed working memory, and dismissing her worry tells her you did not listen.

found-communication-l01.q: A 66-year-old man having chest pain asks you directly, "Am I having a heart attack?" Which reply is both honest and inside your scope?
choices: "Yes, that is what this looks like."
"No, your vitals are fine."
"That is a good question, and the doctor can answer it better than I can. Here is what we are doing right now."
"Try not to think about it."
found-communication-l01.why: Naming what you are doing is true and useful; a diagnosis either way is outside EMT scope and may be wrong. Telling him not to think about it dismisses the fear that is already driving his heart rate up.

found-communication-l02.q: An agitated man is standing between you and the only door of a small bedroom. What is the first thing to fix?
choices: Your position, so that neither of you is cornered and you have a path out
His blood pressure, so you can rule out a medical cause
The lighting in the room
His willingness to sign a refusal
found-communication-l02.why: Personal safety outranks assessment, and a blocked exit is the single finding that should move you before anything else. A cuff mid-argument is unexpected contact, and paperwork is irrelevant while you are trapped.

found-communication-l02.q: A patient's adult daughter is pacing, crying, and repeatedly interrupting your assessment. What is the most useful thing to do with her?
choices: Tell her to wait outside until you are finished
Ignore her and speak louder to the patient
Ask her to gather every medication bottle in the house and bring them to you
Have her sign the patient care report as a witness
found-communication-l02.why: A concrete job returns the control she lost and produces the medication list you need anyway. Removing or ignoring her escalates the room and throws away the best history source for a patient who may not be able to give one.

found-communication-l03.q: A deaf patient tells you in writing that she reads lips. You are wearing a surgical mask. What is the correct next step?
choices: Speak louder and slower through the mask
Request an American Sign Language interpreter, ideally by video
Have her son sign for her
Write the entire consent conversation on a notepad
found-communication-l03.why: A mask removes the lips she is reading, and ASL is a distinct language with its own grammar, so signed English or note passing does not carry a consent conversation. Family interpreting is prohibited for the same reasons it is with spoken languages.

found-communication-l03.q: You walk into a room and the patient speaks only Haitian Creole. What is your first action?
choices: Start the interpreter line while beginning your visual primary survey
Ask the front desk if anyone on shift speaks Creole
Use a translation app to take the full history
Wait for the physician to arrive and handle it
found-communication-l03.why: The delay in language access is almost always logistical, so starting the line immediately while you assess costs nothing. Ad hoc bilingual staff are not qualified interpreters, apps cannot support consent, and waiting stalls the whole call.

found-communication-l04.q: A radio report should run about how long, and what determines what goes in it?
choices: About 2 minutes, so nothing is missed
About 30 seconds, driven by what the listener needs to decide room, team, and speed
About 10 seconds, just age and complaint
As long as it takes to read the chart aloud
found-communication-l04.why: Thirty seconds is the working limit, and every element earns its place by helping the receiving team pick a room and a team. Detail belongs in the written chart and the bedside handoff, not on the air.

found-communication-l04.q: You start your bedside report and the nurse is typing, facing away, and clearly not listening. What do you do?
choices: Talk faster so it takes less of her time
Leave the chart on the bed and clear
Stop, say her name, and wait until she is looking at you before starting
Give the report to the next person who walks by
found-communication-l04.why: A report delivered to someone who is not receiving it transfers nothing, and a handoff is the point where information is most often lost. Leaving paperwork or grabbing a passerby transfers care to no one, which is abandonment.

found-communication-l05.q: A paramedic says, "Give point five of epi." What is wrong with that order as stated?
choices: Nothing, the context makes it clear
A number without a unit is not a dose; ask for the drug, dose with units, and route
Epinephrine is never given in the field
It should have been written down first
found-communication-l05.why: "Point five" could be milligrams or milliliters of very different concentrations, and that ambiguity is exactly how tenfold errors happen. Clarify and read back the complete order before anything is drawn up.

found-communication-l05.q: You notice the nurse is about to give a drug the chart lists as an allergy. What do you do?
choices: Raise it once, and if she keeps going, raise it a second time before escalating
Say it out loud immediately and stop the administration now
Write it in your notes and tell the charge nurse after
Assume she checked and say nothing
found-communication-l05.why: The two-challenge rule is for concerns, not for immediate danger. A documented allergy about to be given is a stop-now event, and waiting for a second challenge or documenting afterward lets the drug reach the patient.

found-communication-l06.q: Your chest pain patient denies shortness of breath and denies nausea. Why write that down?
choices: It makes the narrative longer
Billing requires a minimum word count
They are pertinent negatives: they narrow the picture for the receiving clinician and prove you asked
Only positive findings belong in a chart
found-communication-l06.why: A denied symptom changes what the receiving team considers, and an absent negative reads later as a question never posed. Length and billing have nothing to do with it.

found-communication-l06.q: You apply a tourniquet to a bleeding thigh at 1416. What must appear in the chart?
choices: That a tourniquet was applied
The application time, on its own line, plus the effect on the bleeding
Only the total transport time
The brand of tourniquet
found-communication-l06.why: Tourniquet time drives the receiving surgeon's decisions and is a standing documentation requirement. "A tourniquet was applied" without a time answers none of the questions that get asked later.

found-communication-l07.q: Police place a combative man on a mental health hold and ask you to transport him. Under what type of consent are you operating?
choices: Expressed consent
Implied consent
Involuntary consent
No consent exists, so you cannot transport
found-communication-l07.why: Care authorized by legal authority rather than the patient is involuntary consent, and its requirements vary by state and protocol. Expressed consent requires his agreement and implied consent applies to a patient who simply cannot consent.

found-communication-l07.q: An unconscious crash patient is treated under implied consent. How far does that consent extend?
choices: To any care you judge beneficial, including elective procedures
Only to the care needed for the emergency at hand
To the entire hospital stay
To nothing until a family member signs
found-communication-l07.why: Implied consent assumes a reasonable person would accept lifesaving care, which limits it to the emergency itself. It is not open-ended authorization, and waiting for a signature in a true emergency causes the harm the doctrine exists to prevent.

found-communication-l08.q: Your billing office asks for the patient's full psychiatric history to process a claim for a transport after a fall. What does the minimum necessary standard say?
choices: Provide it; billing is a permitted purpose so the whole chart is fair game
Provide only the information billing needs for this claim, not the unrelated psychiatric history
Provide nothing to billing without written patient authorization
Provide it only if the patient is uninsured
found-communication-l08.why: Payment is a permitted purpose, but each disclosure is capped at what that recipient needs for that purpose. Blanket chart sharing is over-disclosure, and treatment and payment uses do not require written authorization.

found-communication-l08.q: You transport a patient with a gunshot wound to the leg. What is true about reporting it?
choices: Reporting it would violate HIPAA
It may be reported only with the patient's written consent
Gunshot wound reporting is a legally mandated disclosure, with the specifics set by state law and protocol
Only the hospital may ever report it, never EMS
found-communication-l08.why: HIPAA expressly permits disclosures required by law, and gunshot and stab wounds are commonly mandated reports. Consent is not required for a mandated report, and who files it is set by state law rather than being hospital-only by rule.

found-communication-l09.q: An off-duty EMT stops at a collapse, starts CPR, then decides she is late for work and walks away before anyone else arrives. What has occurred?
choices: Nothing, because she had no duty to stop
Abandonment, because beginning care created a duty she then terminated without an equal-or-higher handoff
Battery
False imprisonment
found-communication-l09.why: There may be no duty to stop, but once care begins the duty exists and must continue until someone at an equal or higher level takes over. Battery is unconsented touching and false imprisonment is confinement, neither of which describes leaving.

found-communication-l09.q: Why does gross negligence matter so much to an off-duty provider?
choices: It raises the damages award automatically
It converts a civil case into a criminal one in every state
Good Samaritan protections generally do not cover it, so the immunity disappears
It removes the need to prove causation
found-communication-l09.why: Good Samaritan statutes shield ordinary negligence in good-faith volunteer care and carve out gross negligence and willful misconduct. The plaintiff still must prove all four elements, and criminal exposure is a separate question.

found-communication-l10.q: You have just told a family that their father died. What should happen in the next ten seconds?
choices: Explain the resuscitation in detail so they understand
Nothing from you; stay silent and let them absorb it
Move immediately to funeral home and paperwork questions
Offer a reassuring phrase such as at least it was quick
found-communication-l10.why: Silence is where a shocked brain catches up, and it is the hardest part of the skill. Explanations, logistics, and comfort phrases all fill the space for your benefit rather than theirs.

found-communication-l10.q: A daughter tells you the crew last month "completely botched" her mother's care. What is the correct response?
choices: Agree, so she feels heard
Defend the other crew with what you know of the protocol
Say you cannot speak to what happened before you got here, then state what you are doing now
Suggest she call a lawyer
found-communication-l10.why: You did not witness it, so agreeing or defending is speculation that ends up in a record. Declining to judge and redirecting to current care is honest and keeps the call moving.

found-communication-l11.q: Two patients refuse. One declines an ice pack for a bruised knee; the other declines transport after a head strike while on apixaban. How should your capacity bar differ?
choices: It is identical, because capacity is a fixed threshold
It should be higher for the head strike, because the bar scales with the risk of the decision
It should be lower for the head strike, because he is in more pain
Capacity only applies to medication refusals
found-communication-l11.why: Capacity is decision-specific and the evidence required scales with the stakes, so a possible fatal bleed demands demonstrated understanding of that risk. Pain does not lower the bar, and the same patient can have capacity for one decision and not another.

found-communication-l11.q: A 17-year-old alone at a skate park has a deformed wrist and says he is fine and does not want to go. What is correct?
choices: He may refuse, since 17 is close enough to adult
A bystander adult may refuse for him
He cannot refuse unless emancipated; reach a parent or guardian and document the attempts
Treat and transport without contacting anyone
found-communication-l11.why: New Jersey adulthood begins at 18 and none of the emancipation categories apply here, so a guardian decides. Bystanders hold no authority, and transporting without attempting guardian contact skips a step you will have to prove you took.

found-communication-l12.q: Your narrative ends with "transported without incident." What should replace it?
choices: Transport was uneventful
Patient tolerated transport well
A timed reassessment: repeat vitals with values and any change in the complaint
Nothing; the phrase covers it
found-communication-l12.why: "Without incident" is read later as evidence you did not reassess, and the first two options are the same empty claim reworded. Numbers with a time are the only version that proves monitoring happened.

found-communication-l12.q: You assist a patient with his own nitroglycerin. Beyond dose, route, time, and response, what else must the chart show?
choices: The pharmacy that filled the prescription
The blood pressure documented immediately before administration
The expiration date of the bottle
Your partner's certification number
found-communication-l12.why: Nitroglycerin is pressure-dependent, so the value that authorized the dose has to be in the record. Pharmacy, expiration, and partner credentials do not establish that the administration was appropriate.

found-communication-l13.q: Your first word is cut off on every radio transmission. What is the fix?
choices: Key the microphone, wait one full second, then speak, holding it 2 to 3 inches away
Shout the first word
Hold the microphone against your lips
Repeat the entire report twice
found-communication-l13.why: The radio needs about a second to open the channel, so the pause is the whole solution. Shouting and mouth contact distort the audio, and repeating wastes the 30-second window.

found-communication-l13.q: You are consulting medical control about a high-risk refusal. What must you ask for before you end the call?
choices: The hospital's bed availability
The physician's name, for your documentation
An estimated wait time in the emergency department
The patient's insurance status
found-communication-l13.why: A verbal consult you cannot attribute to a named physician is worth very little later, so the name and the time go in the chart. Bed counts, wait times, and insurance have no bearing on the refusal record.

found-communication-l14.q: A local news reporter at a crash scene asks you what happened to the patient. What do you say?
choices: Give the mechanism but no clinical details
Give the age and condition without the name
"I cannot discuss patients," and refer them to the public information officer
Answer fully, since the crash happened in public
found-communication-l14.why: There is no treatment, payment, or operations purpose in a press inquiry, so the single sentence and a referral is the whole answer. Partial details still identify a patient at an identifiable scene.

found-communication-l14.q: A patient's adult daughter, named as the health care representative in a proxy directive, asks about her mother's condition. What is correct?
choices: Decline, because family may never receive clinical information
Verify her identity and the role, then share what her authority covers
Share everything immediately, since she is family
Share only after the patient regains consciousness and consents
found-communication-l14.why: A named representative has real authority, but it only applies once identity and role are verified. Blanket refusal ignores a lawful decision maker, and unverified disclosure to anyone claiming the role is the classic breach.

found-communication-l15.q: A physician on the radio says, "Give him some oxygen and whatever else he needs." What do you do?
choices: Act on your best interpretation and document it
Ask for the specific drug, dose, route, and conditions, then read back the clarified order
Decline the whole consult and transport
Ask your partner what the physician meant
found-communication-l15.why: Vague direction is not an order, and it gets clarified before you act rather than explained afterward. Interpreting it yourself puts you outside any authorization, and your partner cannot clarify what the physician said.

found-communication-l15.q: Before you key the microphone to reach medical control, what should already be decided?
choices: Exactly what you are requesting, in one sentence
Which hospital has the shortest wait
Whether your partner agrees with the plan
What the patient's insurance will cover
found-communication-l15.why: A physician who has never seen this patient has to decide in under a minute, so a report with no clear ask wastes the call. Wait times, crew consensus, and coverage do not shape the order you are seeking.

found-communication-l16.q: After a medication error you file an incident report. How should the patient care report reference it?
choices: Attach a copy of the incident report to the chart
Write "incident report filed" in the narrative
Not at all; the chart records the clinical facts, the notification, and the response
Write the word error in bold so reviewers find it
found-communication-l16.why: The incident report belongs to a separate quality process and referencing it drags that process into the medical record. The chart carries what was given, when, the patient's response, and who was notified.

found-communication-l16.q: A technician skips the second patient identifier because the department is slammed and she has done it a hundred times without a problem. How does just culture classify this?
choices: Human error, calling for system repair and support
At-risk behavior, calling for coaching and removal of the incentive to shortcut
Reckless behavior, calling for discipline
Not a safety issue at all
found-communication-l16.why: A shortcut whose risk has drifted out of view is at-risk behavior, which is coached rather than punished. Human error is an unintended slip, and reckless behavior is conscious disregard of a known serious risk, such as working impaired.

found-communication-l17.q: You tell a patient her test was "negative." Why is that risky wording?
choices: It is too technical for any patient
Many patients hear negative as bad news, the reverse of the clinical meaning
It is legally inadmissible
It only applies to imaging results
found-communication-l17.why: Negative and positive carry opposite everyday meanings from their clinical ones, which is why plain phrasing such as "the test did not find it" is safer. The words are common, not technical, and the problem is comprehension, not law.

found-communication-l17.q: You need to describe a 2.5 cm laceration to a frightened patient. What phrasing follows the lesson?
choices: "You have a 2.5 centimeter laceration."
"You have a superficial soft tissue disruption."
"It is a cut about the size of a quarter."
"It is nothing, do not worry about it."
found-communication-l17.why: A familiar comparison lands faster than a measurement for a stressed listener. Jargon fails the vocabulary test and minimizing the injury dismisses the concern that brought them in.

quiz.q: You crouch beside a 74-year-old woman who fell in her bathroom and ask, "Are you having any pain, dizziness, nausea, or trouble breathing?" She answers, "No trouble breathing." What went wrong?
choices: You should have addressed her as sweetie to build rapport
You should have stood over her so she could hear you
You stacked four questions, and a frightened patient answers only the last one
You should have asked her family instead
quiz.why: Stacked questions produce an answer to the final item and nothing else, because fear shrinks working memory. Diminutives read as condescending, standing over a patient reads as dominance, and going to family first takes her voice away.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old man with crushing chest pain grips your wrist and asks whether he is going to die. Which response is best?
choices: "I am going to stay with you. Here is exactly what we are doing right now."
"You are going to be fine, do not worry."
"I cannot answer that."
"Probably not, most people with chest pain are fine."
quiz.why: Staying and narrating are both true and both reduce fear without promising an outcome you cannot guarantee. A flat refusal to engage closes the door, and reassurance about statistics is a prognosis you are not qualified to give.

quiz.q: A patient is seated on a low couch and you are standing in front of her with your clipboard. What should you change first?
choices: Your tone of voice
The order of your questions
The amount of detail in your explanations
Your height, by crouching or sitting so you are at eye level
quiz.why: Standing over a seated patient is read as a power position regardless of intent, and dropping to eye level changes the interaction immediately. Tone, sequence, and detail all matter, but none of them fixes the physical dynamic.

quiz.q: A confused, sweaty 70-year-old man is swinging at your partner in his kitchen. Before you treat this as a behavioral emergency, what must you do?
choices: Ask the family whether he has a psychiatric history
Check a blood glucose and a pulse oximetry reading and consider head injury and intoxication
Request police and wait outside
Apply restraints for everyone's safety
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia and hypoxia produce exactly this picture and are both fixable in minutes, which is why they are ruled out first. A psychiatric history does not exclude a medical cause, and restraining a hypoxic patient is how people die in restraints.

quiz.q: A man in a small apartment is shouting at your crew. Three of you are answering him at once. What is the single most useful change?
choices: Raise your voices so you can be heard over him
Have one crew member with the best rapport speak while the others stop talking
Move closer so he can hear you better
Tell him police are on the way
quiz.why: Three people reasoning at once reads as an ambush and raises arousal. Matching volume escalates, closing distance removes his space, and a police threat is a threat rather than a de-escalation.

quiz.q: A patient tells you men are transmitting messages through his ceiling. What is the best reply?
choices: "There is nobody up there, you are imagining it."
"I hear them too, let us get you out of here."
"I do not see them, but I believe you are scared, and I want to help with that."
"We can talk about that at the hospital."
quiz.why: You neither argue with the delusion nor agree with it; you acknowledge the fear, which is the part that is real to him. Contradiction provokes a fight, collusion reinforces the delusion, and deflection tells him you are not listening.

quiz.q: A Portuguese-speaking patient's husband insists on interpreting and answers before she finishes speaking. The interpreter line is available. What is the safest reading of this situation?
choices: He is being efficient and should continue
Family interpretation is acceptable if the patient agrees
Use him, then confirm with the interpreter at the hospital
Use the qualified interpreter and get a private moment with the patient
quiz.why: Family members edit, and a partner who answers for the patient is exactly the pattern that hides coercion or abuse. Deferring verification to the hospital leaves you without valid consent now and without the disclosure she could only make privately.

quiz.q: Through a phone interpreter you say, "Does it feel like an elephant is sitting on your chest?" The patient looks baffled. What is the problem?
choices: The interpreter is unqualified
Idioms do not translate; ask whether it feels heavy or squeezing
The question should have been directed to the interpreter
Chest pain questions require a video interpreter
quiz.why: Idiomatic phrasing becomes nonsense in many languages, while plain descriptors translate cleanly. The interpreter is doing her job, speaking to the patient is correct, and the modality is not what broke here.

quiz.q: After explaining a procedure through an interpreter, the patient nods. What must you do before proceeding?
choices: Ask her to say in her own words what is going to happen
Ask the interpreter whether the patient understood
Ask a family member to confirm
Nothing; a nod is agreement
quiz.why: Teach-back is the only way to know comprehension happened, and a nod is politeness. The interpreter conveys words rather than judging understanding, and family confirmation reintroduces the exact bias you removed.

quiz.q: You are five minutes out with a 71-year-old woman whose face drooped 40 minutes ago. Which element most changes what the hospital does before you arrive?
choices: Her home address
Her medication allergies
Her past surgical history
The time she was last known well, and a stroke alert request
quiz.why: Last known well determines treatment eligibility and mobilizes the stroke team before the doors open, which is the entire purpose of the call. Allergies and surgical history matter later, and the address never belongs on the radio.

quiz.q: An ED tech gives this report: "Bed 6 is a 54-year-old with abdominal pain, history of diverticulitis, pressure is 92 over 54, down from 128 over 78 an hour ago, and he looks gray." What is missing?
choices: The situation
The recommendation
The background
The assessment
quiz.why: Situation, background, and assessment are all present; what is absent is the request, such as asking the nurse to come see him now. Without a stated ask the listener has to guess what you want, which is why nothing happens.

quiz.q: You are handing off a motorcyclist thrown 30 feet. Which sentence should come first?
choices: "He has no allergies and takes no medications."
"His wife is following us in a car."
"Motorcycle versus guardrail at highway speed, rider thrown roughly 30 feet."
"We started an IV en route."
quiz.why: MIST leads with mechanism because it predicts the injuries the trauma team has not yet found. Medications, family logistics, and interventions all follow once the team knows what they are preparing for.

quiz.q: In a resuscitation you call out, "Somebody grab the suction." Nothing happens. Why?
choices: The team did not hear you over the noise
Suction is not part of a resuscitation
Diffusion of responsibility; a task assigned to no one in particular gets done by no one
You should have written the order down
quiz.why: When an instruction is aimed at the room, everyone assumes someone else has it. Naming a person and giving one task is the fix, and volume and paperwork do not address the mechanism.

quiz.q: You have administered aspirin as ordered. What closes the loop?
choices: Charting it at the end of the call
Announcing it out loud with the time, such as "aspirin 324 milligrams given at 1412"
Telling the patient it has been given
Placing the empty packet in the ordering provider's view
quiz.why: The team does not know an intervention happened until someone says so, and the time is part of the information. Charting later, informing the patient, and leaving a visual cue all leave the sender uncertain in the moment.

quiz.q: Which of these is offline medical direction?
choices: A physician on the phone authorizing a second nitroglycerin dose
A radio consult about terminating a resuscitation
The regional protocol authorizing oral glucose for a conscious hypoglycemic patient
A physician giving directions by video from the emergency department
quiz.why: Offline direction is the medical director's authorization issued in advance in writing. The other three are all live physician contact during the call, which is online direction.

quiz.q: Which narrative line is written as an observation rather than a conclusion?
choices: Patient was clearly faking the pain
Patient was hostile from the start
Patient seemed anxious but was probably fine
Patient paced the room, spoke in short phrases, and stated "I cannot sit still"
quiz.why: Behaviors and a direct quote are verifiable and let the reader draw the conclusion. The other three are judgments about the patient that a reviewer or attorney can attack directly.

quiz.q: A partner asks you to document that a set of vitals was taken at 1430 when it was actually taken at 1450. What should you do?
choices: Document it as requested, since the difference is small
Document the actual time and decline; charting a time you did not obtain is falsification
Leave the time blank
Document both times and let a reviewer decide
quiz.why: Recording something that did not happen as written is falsification regardless of how small the change is, and timing is frequently the central question later. Blank or contradictory entries create their own problems without fixing the ethical one.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs in the patient care report but is most often omitted?
choices: The chief complaint
The transport destination
The response to each intervention
The patient's date of birth
quiz.why: Providers routinely record what was given and stop, leaving no evidence of whether it worked. Complaint, destination, and identifiers are captured almost automatically by every reporting system.

quiz.q: Halfway down a paper PCR you realize you have been charting on the wrong patient's form. What is the correct handling?
choices: Line through the erroneous entries so they remain readable, initial and date them, and complete the correct form
Shred the form and start over
White out the entries and reuse the form
Write over the entries with the correct information
quiz.why: A single line preserves the original while showing who changed what and when. Destroying, obliterating, or overwriting a record all look like concealment even when the intent was innocent.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old with an oxygen saturation of 84 percent is confused and pulling off the mask, insisting he wants to go home. What is the correct action?
choices: Honor the refusal, since he is speaking clearly
Have him sign a refusal and document the saturation
Treat under implied consent, because hypoxia has removed his capacity, and contact medical direction
Ask his neighbor to make the decision
quiz.why: Hypoxia impairs the reasoning capacity requires, so this is not a valid refusal, and correcting the oxygen often restores the ability to decide. A neighbor holds no authority, and a signature from someone without capacity protects nobody.

quiz.q: Which statement about capacity is correct?
choices: It is decided by a judge and applies to all decisions
It is decision-specific, so a patient may have it for one choice and lack it for another
It is established by scoring alert and oriented times four
It cannot be assessed by an EMT
quiz.why: Capacity is a bedside clinical judgment about this decision at this moment, which is why the same patient can hold it for a minor choice and lack it for a high-risk one. Competence is the court determination, and orientation is only one input.

quiz.q: A patient with a valid POLST that specifies comfort-focused treatment is in respiratory distress with a pulse. What is appropriate?
choices: No care at all, since the form limits treatment
Chest compressions
Immediate intubation regardless of the form
Oxygen, positioning, suctioning, and comfort measures, consistent with the form
quiz.why: A POLST limits specified interventions but never withholds comfort, oxygen, or symptom relief. Compressions are wrong in a patient with a pulse, ignoring the form overrides a valid medical order, and doing nothing misreads what the document says.

quiz.q: A nursing home produces a DNR, but the patient's son at the bedside demands full resuscitation. The patient is in arrest. What do you do?
choices: Honor the son's wishes without further action
Begin resuscitation and contact medical direction immediately
Honor the DNR and ignore the son
Wait for the facility administrator to arrive
quiz.why: A contested order is treated as doubt, and the default in doubt is to start while a physician sorts it out. You can always stop resuscitation, but the minutes lost to waiting or to a bedside argument cannot be recovered.

quiz.q: You need to leave a message for a patient's spouse. Which detail most clearly makes a voicemail a disclosure risk?
choices: Stating your first name
Stating the time you are calling
Stating the diagnosis and the room number
Stating that you are returning a call
quiz.why: A diagnosis tied to a location is protected health information reaching a device you cannot verify. Your name, the time, and a callback reference disclose nothing about the patient's condition.

quiz.q: Which of these is the most common way technicians actually commit a HIPAA breach?
choices: Selling records to a third party
Convenience and volume, such as hallway conversations and unattended charts
Hacking another department's system
Refusing to release records to a court
quiz.why: The everyday breaches are not malicious; they are the byproduct of being busy, which is why the safeguards are physical and habitual. Selling records and hacking are rare criminal acts, and refusing a lawful order is a different problem entirely.

quiz.q: You are told a well-known local athlete is in the department. A coworker not assigned to him opens his chart and calls you over to look. What is your obligation?
choices: Look, since your coworker already opened it
Look but do not repeat anything
Decline to look, and understand that both of you would be creating an auditable breach
Look only at the vitals, which are not protected
quiz.why: Access requires a treatment, payment, or operations relationship, and every view is logged with a user ID. There is no partial-access exception, and vitals are protected health information like anything else in the chart.

quiz.q: A nurse tells you a 3-year-old's spiral arm fracture does not match the parent's story, and asks you to report it since you were on the transport. Which statement is correct?
choices: Only physicians may report suspected child abuse in New Jersey
You must wait for the hospital's investigation to conclude
You should report only if the nurse also reports
New Jersey requires any person with reasonable cause to report immediately to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE
quiz.why: New Jersey is a universal mandated reporting state, so the obligation is personal and does not depend on anyone else's action. Waiting for an investigation or for another provider's report delays protection for the child.

quiz.q: An EMT performs a skill outside her certification level, and the patient recovers fully with no harm. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: No issue arises, because the outcome was good
Negligence is established by the scope violation alone
She committed battery
Negligence likely fails for lack of damages, but the scope violation is still a certification problem
quiz.why: All four negligence elements are required and damages are absent here, but acting outside a state-defined scope is a separate regulatory matter that a good outcome does not cure. Battery requires unconsented touching, which this vignette does not describe.

quiz.q: A crew transports a competent adult who has clearly and repeatedly refused. What has occurred?
choices: Abandonment
Implied consent
False imprisonment
Gross negligence, automatically
quiz.why: Confining and moving someone against their will is false imprisonment, and consent is the protection. Abandonment is ending care improperly, implied consent applies only to a patient who cannot consent, and gross negligence is a separate standard requiring reckless disregard.

quiz.q: Which element of negligence is missing when an EMT who was never dispatched drives past a collapsed pedestrian in a state with no duty to stop?
choices: Damages
Duty
Breach
Causation
quiz.why: Without an obligation to this person there is no duty, and the claim fails at the first element. Harm may well exist and causation may be arguable, but neither matters once duty is absent.

quiz.q: A paramedic transfers a patient who needs only splinting and transport to an EMT crew. Is this abandonment?
choices: No, because the patient's needs fall within the EMT scope
Yes, because any downward transfer is abandonment
Yes, unless the patient signs a consent form
Only if the patient later deteriorates
quiz.why: Transfer to a lower level is acceptable when the patient's needs are within that level's scope. Abandonment arises when the receiving level cannot meet the patient's actual needs, not from the direction of the transfer alone.

quiz.q: A widow asks whether her husband suffered during his cardiac arrest. You did not witness the collapse. What is the honest answer?
choices: "He was in terrible pain, but it was quick."
"He lost consciousness within seconds and was not aware of anything, and the doctor can tell you more."
"Nobody can ever know that."
"He probably felt everything, I am sorry."
quiz.why: You can truthfully state that an arrest patient loses awareness within seconds, then hand the rest to the physician. Speculating in either direction invents a fact and creates guilt or horror that lasts decades.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old is stable on her mother's lap while you take a history. Her mother is calm. What is the best positioning?
choices: Move the child to the stretcher immediately for a proper exam
Keep the child on the mother's lap and explain each step before you do it
Ask the mother to step out so the child focuses on you
Have the mother hold the child facing away so she cannot see you
quiz.why: A stable child on a trusted adult stays calmer, which produces a better exam, and announcing each step prevents startle. Separating the two or hiding your hands both raise the child's fear and the mother's.

quiz.q: A husband has been shouting at you about your response time for 20 seconds. What should you be doing?
choices: Correcting his estimate of how long it took
Asking him to leave the room
Explaining the dispatch and routing decisions
Listening without defending, then naming the emotion and acknowledging the experience
quiz.why: Interrupting to correct a fact resets the clock and hardens the anger, while listening and naming defuses it and buys you the medication list. Removing him escalates and costs you your best source of history.

quiz.q: An intoxicated 30-year-old who struck his head says, "If I stay home I could bleed in my head and die overnight, and I am accepting that. I want to sleep in my own bed." Vitals are normal, glucose 96. What does this demonstrate?
choices: He lacks capacity because he has been drinking
He has demonstrated the understanding and reasoning capacity requires for this decision
Capacity cannot be assessed in anyone who has consumed alcohol
A breath alcohol test is required before you can decide
quiz.why: Capacity is functional, and stating the specific risk and accepting it is exactly the evidence you are looking for. Alcohol neither removes nor preserves capacity automatically, and no measured level decides it.

quiz.q: A 79-year-old with mild dementia wants to decline an ice pack for a bruised shin. Her caregiver confirms she is at her usual baseline. What is reasonable?
choices: Treat her as having no capacity for any decision
Require her guardian to approve every choice
Accept the refusal of the ice pack, since capacity is decision-specific and this is a low-risk choice
Transport her under implied consent
quiz.why: Dementia is a spectrum, not a switch, and the evidence required scales with the stakes of the decision. Blanket incapacity and implied consent for a bruise both override a patient who can reasonably make this particular choice.

quiz.q: Which refusal vignette should immediately raise the question of absent capacity?
choices: A 40-year-old with a sprained ankle who wants to drive himself to urgent care
A 30-year-old who declines an ice pack after a minor burn
A 25-year-old who declines a second set of vitals
A 55-year-old diabetic with a glucose of 41 who insists he is fine
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia directly impairs the reasoning capacity requires and is the classic exam trigger, along with hypoxia, head injury, and significant intoxication. The other three describe low-stakes choices by patients with no impairment described.

quiz.q: Which chart entry gives the receiving clinician usable information?
choices: Patient was stable throughout
Vitals were within normal limits
No acute distress noted
SpO2 rose from 91 percent on room air at 1422 to 97 percent on 2 liters nasal cannula at 1435
quiz.why: Two timed values show both the problem and the response to what you did. The other three are summaries with no content, and stable in particular is read later as evidence that no reassessment occurred.

quiz.q: You are writing a narrative for a patient who shouted and swore at you. What is the defensible way to capture it?
choices: Write that the patient was verbally abusive and hostile
Omit the behavior entirely to protect the patient
Quote the statements and describe the observed behavior without characterizing the patient
Write that the patient has an anger problem
quiz.why: Quotes and behaviors are evidence; labels are opinions that damage the chart and bias the patient's later care. Omitting clinically relevant behavior removes information the receiving team may need for safety.

quiz.q: When should the narrative for a call be written?
choices: Before you clear, while the times are still accurate
At the end of the shift, when there is time to write well
Within 24 hours, once you have reflected on the call
Only if something unusual happened
quiz.why: Reconstructed times are the first thing challenged later, and memory for sequence degrades within the hour. Every call gets a narrative, not just the unusual ones.

quiz.q: Which radio transmission is written correctly?
choices: "Be advised we have a frequent flyer for you again."
"68-year-old female, alert, tripoding, respirations 28, saturation 88 percent on room air now 94 percent on CPAP, one albuterol given with partial improvement, requesting a respiratory-ready room."
"We have a really sick lady, you will see when we get there."
"Bringing in Mrs. Delgado from 14 Oak Street with breathing trouble."
quiz.why: Age, severity, numbers, treatment response, and a specific request are exactly what the receiving team needs to assign a room and a team. The others transmit a label, no data, or identifiers that never belong on a recorded channel.

quiz.q: Which item is unique to the trauma report and drives the trauma team's preparation most?
choices: Mechanism, including speed, restraint use, intrusion, and ejection
The patient's oxygen saturation
The estimated time of arrival
The treatment given en route
quiz.why: Mechanism predicts injuries nobody has seen yet, which is why MIST puts it first. Saturation, ETA, and treatment appear in every report regardless of call type.

quiz.q: A pediatric radio report should include which element that an adult report does not?
choices: Blood pressure
Chief complaint
Weight in kilograms
Level of consciousness
quiz.why: Weight drives every pediatric drug dose and every equipment size, so the receiving team needs it before arrival. Pressure, complaint, and mental status belong in reports at any age.

quiz.q: You are teaching a class and want to use a difficult call as an example. What makes it permissible?
choices: Changing the patient's first name
Getting verbal permission from your partner
Saying that the patient will never find out
Removing the name, date, location, and every other detail that could identify the patient
quiz.why: Genuinely de-identified information is no longer protected health information, and education is an operations purpose. A pseudonym, a colleague's blessing, and the patient's ignorance change nothing about identifiability.

quiz.q: A caller says he is the patient's brother and asks which hospital you transported to. What is correct?
choices: Do not disclose from the field; identity cannot be verified by phone and facility directory rules govern what may be confirmed
Confirm the hospital but nothing else
Confirm it if he can name the patient's date of birth
Confirm it since hospital location is public information
quiz.why: Confirming a destination confirms that the person is a patient, which is itself a disclosure to an unverified caller. Knowing a date of birth is not identity verification, and the hospital's own directory policy decides what a facility may confirm.

quiz.q: Which of these is a permitted disclosure under HIPAA?
choices: Texting a scene photo to an off-duty coworker who was curious
Telling a first responder crew the outcome of a patient they lifted last week
Reviewing a call with your supervisor for quality improvement
Telling a patient's employer why he was transported
quiz.why: Quality improvement review is a health care operations purpose, expressly permitted. The other three go to people with no treatment, payment, or operations role in this patient's care.

quiz.q: You need physician authorization to assist a patient with a second nitroglycerin dose. Which call opening is best?
choices: "Doc, we have a guy here with chest pain, what do you want us to do?"
"Medic 3 requesting online medical direction, 62-year-old male with chest pain, and I am requesting permission to assist with a second dose of his own nitroglycerin."
"Medic 3, we are going to give another nitro unless you say otherwise."
"Medic 3, calling to update you on our chest pain patient."
quiz.why: Identifying yourself and stating the specific ask lets a physician who has never seen this patient decide quickly. An open-ended question wastes the window, assuming approval is not a request, and an update carries no decision point.

quiz.q: A physician orders nitroglycerin. You look down and the systolic pressure is 84. What is the best response?
choices: Give it, since the physician has the authority
Refuse and end the transmission
Give it and document your objection afterward
"Doctor, I want to be sure you have this: his systolic is 84 and he is diaphoretic. Do you still want the nitroglycerin?"
quiz.why: Leading with the observation usually reveals the detail the physician did not have, which is the common explanation. Giving a pressure-dependent drug at that systolic risks real harm, and silence or a flat refusal forfeits the chance to fix it.

quiz.q: After carrying out a verbal order, what must appear in the chart?
choices: That the order came from medical control
The ordering physician's name, the exact order, the time given, the time performed, and the patient's response
The radio frequency used
A note that your partner heard the order too
quiz.why: A verbal order you cannot attribute to a named physician with a time is very hard to defend later, and the response completes the record. A generic reference to medical control, a frequency, or a witness does not establish who authorized what.

quiz.q: You gave a correct medication to the wrong patient during a busy transport. The patient is fine. What comes first?
choices: Assess the patient and tell the receiving clinician immediately
File the agency incident report
Tell your supervisor
Write the event into the narrative
quiz.why: The clinician taking over needs the information now to watch for effects, so patient safety precedes every reporting step. Supervisor notification, the incident report, and documentation all follow.

quiz.q: A near miss is best described as which of the following?
choices: An error that reached the patient but caused no harm
A complaint that did not become a lawsuit
An error caught before it reached the patient
A deviation from protocol that a supervisor approved
quiz.why: A near miss never touches the patient, which is precisely what makes it a free lesson for the system. An error that reached the patient without harm is a safety event, and the other two are not error categories at all.

quiz.q: A nurse dismisses your report that a patient's pressure fell from 124 to 88 in ten minutes. What is the correct next step?
choices: Accept her judgment and keep monitoring quietly
State the number again with your specific request, and if it is still not addressed, escalate up the chain
Document that you told her and continue your assigned tasks
Raise your voice so the physician overhears
quiz.why: The two-challenge rule gives you a second, clearer attempt and then requires escalation, because deference to a deteriorating patient is not professionalism. Quiet monitoring and documentation alone leave the patient untreated, and performing for the room is not escalation.

quiz.q: You hand a patient discharge instructions and she says she will read them at home. What is the best response?
choices: Accept it; adults can read their own instructions
Ask directly whether she has trouble reading
Read the key line aloud as your routine for everyone, then teach-back the one action that matters most
Give the instructions to a family member instead
quiz.why: Deferring to read later is a common sign of low literacy, and a routine that applies to everyone removes the embarrassment. Asking directly shames her, handing the paper to family takes away her control, and accepting it leaves comprehension unverified.

quiz.q: During a phone interpretation, a patient speaks for 30 seconds and the interpreter returns three words. What should you say?
choices: Nothing; interpreters compress for efficiency
Ask the patient to repeat herself more briefly
"Please give me everything she said, word for word."
Switch to a family member for the rest of the call
quiz.why: Summarized interpretation drops exactly the detail you are trying to collect, and asking for verbatim relay is both appropriate and expected. Shortening the patient's answers and swapping in family both make the information loss worse.
